analysis.one_liner: Repeals the 3.8% Medicare tax on high earners' investment income.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee in April 2011 and never received a committee vote; it died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have deleted the 3.8% tax on investment income — interest, dividends, capital gains — that high earners owe on top of their regular taxes. That tax, created as part of the 2010 health care law, applies to couples earning over $250,000 a year and sends its revenue to Medicare. The bill never got so much as a committee vote: it was sent to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and stayed there until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households with investment income. A couple earning over $250,000 with dividends, capital gains, or rental income would pay 3.8% less tax on that income, with the largest dollar savings going to those with the biggest investment portfolios.

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes the entire chapter of the tax code containing the unearned income Medicare contribution, repealing the 3.8% tax on net investment income beginning with tax years after December 31, 2012.
The tax being repealed applies only to net investment income, meaning high earners' gains from investments rather than wages — so the benefit is concentrated among households with large portfolios.
Repeal is retroactive in design to apply to years after 2012, maximizing the cumulative savings for taxpayers who hold the most investment income.

analysis.who_pays: The Medicare trust fund, which loses a dedicated revenue stream, and by extension everyone who relies on Medicare — the tax was created specifically to help finance the program. Ordinary taxpayers who benefit from Medicare's solvency bear the difference.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicare's funding and its future beneficiaries

drawbacks.text: Repealing the tax removes a dedicated revenue stream that was created to shore up Medicare financing, shifting the burden of keeping the program solvent back onto general revenues or future benefit cuts.

The tax only applies above roughly $200,000 for single filers and $250,000 for couples, so repeal delivers no benefit at all to households below those thresholds while cutting bills most for those at the top.
An honest supporter would have to acknowledge the revenue loss: Medicare is projected to face financing shortfalls, and this was one of the few dedicated funding streams added to address them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits flow almost entirely to high-income households, and the cost — a smaller Medicare funding base — is spread across everyone who depends on the program. For ordinary working people, the costs outweigh the benefits.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a markup or floor vote; it died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Grimm introduced the bill on April 14, 2011.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tax legislation.
Twenty members cosponsored the bill — 19 Republicans and 1 Democrat — showing substantial support within the chamber.
No further action was ever taken; the action history ends with the committee referral, and the bill expired with the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare's dedicated funding stream survived intact, and the 3.8% tax continues to apply to high earners' investment income. The households the bill would have benefited — those with the largest investment portfolios — did not get the tax cut.

for.name: Rep. Michael Grimm
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to repeal the 3.8% unearned income Medicare contribution and referred it to committee.

against.name: Rep. Dave Camp
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or vote during the two-year Congress.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after the referral; no markup, no vote, no report.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Republican: 19 of the bill's 20 cosponsors were Republicans, with one Democrat, and the bill never advanced in a committee chaired by a member of the sponsoring party.

industries.note: Repeal would cut the 3.8% tax these households pay on dividends, capital gains, and other investment income — with the biggest savings going to the largest portfolios. The public's cost is the same money, which was earmarked to help finance Medicare.
The tax is a dedicated Medicare financing stream; repeal would weaken the program's funding, a cost borne by the tens of millions of people who rely on it.
